item.content:encoded:
”Lomu”, a documentary that tells the life story of the late rugby legend Jonah Lomu will be screened publicly for the first time in Nuku’alofa at Teufaiva Stadium on Wednesday, 29 July.

The documentary was directed by award-winning Tongan-New Zealand filmmaker Vea Mafile’o, with co-director Gavin Fitzgerald, who is based in Ireland. Vea wants to celebrate the life of the rugby legend through the documentary.

Vea’s father comes from Tongoleleka, Ha’apai, and is a rugby man who used to coach rugby at Toloa. Her co-director, Gavin, also loves rugby and grew up adoring Jonah.

“Everyone in overseas, especially in England, loves Jonah. He is really quite popular. Obviously, nowadays, not as popular as before, but the majority of people over there definitely already know him. So it was an exciting project in terms of working with a production company from England and a production company from New Zealand and us coming together to create the story,” she said.

Vea said they interviewed Lomu’s family and close friends, as well as coaches from the rugby world.

“It was very important for us to involve his family, especially his mother and his brother, John.”

“What was really enlightening for me was the understanding that he was this man in the center and then there’s lots of different moving parts; family, rugby, the world, that complicated his life. But he was actually just a very kind hearted — normal Tongan boy.”

She said the role of the media and the people around him put things out there that were not very fair.

“It was important for me to try and unpick some of those narratives that had already been put out there and just to give us that opportunity to celebrate him, because this is the missing piece. We’ve never had the chance to celebrate him as the son of Tonga, and as a son of New Zealand as well, because it’s always been negative.”

Parts of the documentary were filmed in New Zealand, while other scenes were filmed in Tonga at Anahulu.

Vea said it was important to bring more Tongan culture into the documentary and create a narrative that is not the norm for a sports documentary.

Actor, songwriter and artist, JP Foliaki said, “We want people here to see it because we feel that they deserve to see it first.”

Lomu has only been screened at an Australian film festival and a few other film festivals, but this will be the first time it will be shown to the public.

“So that’s going to be essentially making history,” he said,

The public is invited to attend the free documentary screening at Teufaiva Stadium at 5:00 pm on Wednesday, 29 July.

Jonah Lomu died at the age of 40 in New Zealand, 11 years ago this November.

The 1.96-metre (6ft 5in) Jonah made his Test debut in 1994 against France in Christchurch. He earned 63 caps for the All Blacks.

As a global superstar of rugby union, he had a huge impact on the game. He was inducted into the International Rugby Hall of Fame on 9 October 2007 and the IRB Hall of Fame on 24 October 2011.

Lomu was appointed a Member of the New Zealand Order of Merit in the Queen’s Birthday Honours list on 4 June 2007.

His parents emigrated from Tonga to New Zealand, where Jonah was born on 12 May 1975. He attended Wesley College in Auckland.

item.title: U-18 titles for Liahona High School Girls and 'Apifo'ou College Boys
item.description: Apifo'ou College secured a third consecutive Tonga secondary schools U-18 boys football title after defeating Tonga College in a dramatic penalty shootout following a 3-3 draw in the final at the weekend. The championship decider was one of the tournament's most memorable matches, with Apifo'ou prevailing from the spot after extra-time was not played. It was the third final of the day to be decide
item.content:encoded:
Apifo'ou College secured a third consecutive Tonga secondary schools U-18 boys football title after defeating Tonga College in a dramatic penalty shootout following a 3-3 draw in the final at the weekend.

The championship decider was one of the tournament's most memorable matches, with Apifo'ou prevailing from the spot after extra-time was not played. It was the third final of the day to be decided on penalties.

Apifo'ou made the ideal start when Tevita Falepapalangi won and converted an early penalty after being fouled inside the area, giving the defending champions a 1-0 halftime lead. They extended their advantage after the restart through winger Hakeai Fonua, whose composed finish made it 2-0 and appeared to put Apifo'ou in control.

Tonga College responded strongly, led by Maama Makoni, who scored twice from free kicks to level the scores at 2-2 and swing momentum in his side's favour.

Falepapalangi restored Apifo'ou's lead with an impressive solo effort, weaving past several defenders before finishing calmly to make it 3-2. The forward's celebrations proved costly, however, as he received a second yellow card for removing his shirt after scoring, leaving the defending champions to finish the match with 10 players.

Tonga College capitalised on the advantage, with striker Sitaleki Kautai scoring a late equaliser to force a penalty shootout.

Both teams converted their opening four penalties before Tonga College missed their decisive attempt. Apifo'ou then converted the winning spot kick to complete a 5-4 shootout victory and seal a third successive championship.

The final highlighted the depth of emerging football talent in Tonga, with several players from both schools recently representing the Tonga U-19 men's national team at the OFC U-19 Men's Qualifying Tournament in the Cook Islands.

Liahona High School claimed the U-18 girls title

Liahona High School successfully defended the U-18 girls title with a commanding 6-0 victory over Takuilau College.

Liahona dominated from the opening whistle, building a 4-0 halftime lead through an organised attacking display led by forward 'Anamalia Vahe.

The defending champions maintained control after the break, adding two more goals to complete an emphatic victory and retain the U-18 girls crown.

The result capped another successful campaign for Liahona, who claimed back-to-back titles with an unbeaten run through the competition.

item.title: Glasgow baptism of fire adds fuel to Tonga Tala's quest
item.description: Netball star Uneeq Palavi says Tonga are viewing a tough loss to Australia at the Commonwealth Games as a step closer to putting their country on the map. Palavi won't beat around the bush, a 61-goal loss to the Diamonds at the Commonwealth Games was tough to swallow.
item.content:encoded:
Netball star Uneeq Palavi says Tonga are viewing a tough loss to Australia at the Commonwealth Games as a step closer to putting their country on the map.

Palavi won't beat around the bush, a 61-goal loss to the Diamonds at the Commonwealth Games was tough to swallow.

But goalscorer Palavi knows there'll be plenty of rough times ahead as the Tala attempt to climb netball's summit and put "our little country on the map".

On Games debut in Glasgow, Tonga endured a baptism of fire in their opening match against perennial heavyweights Australia.

World No.8 Tonga were simply no match for the four-time Games gold medallists, with former Melbourne Mavericks shooter Palavi unable to flaunt her quality in attack against the rock-solid Diamonds defence.

" We were pretty much telling ourselves, 'Oh, we're going to beat the Diamonds'. Just the hype-up," Palavi joked.

" It wasn't the best, but to come up against the world's best is obviously going to be something like that.

" We're not a new team, but we're new in this environment.

" I feel like it's a lot to come up against the world's best and put out what we wanted to.

" It's just another step closer to putting our little country on the map, and I feel like that's all that matters."

Tonga's bid for a boilover continues when they face South Africa on Monday morning ( AEST ) before taking on Northern Ireland.

She was Tonga's top scorer and fourth overall as her side finished eighth at the 2023 World Cup.

The island nation - which boasts a population of just over 100,000 - sit ahead of Games hosts world No.10 Scotland and behind No.7 Wales in the world rankings.

And while the Tala may have been playing nearly 20,000 kilometres away from home, they still had plenty of support at the Hydro.

" I didn't expect so many Tongans to be out there, but that's the crazy thing about it," Palavi said after the 99-38 defeat.

" No matter where in the world you are, there's always Tongans to support."

Defending their 2022 Birmingham gold medal, Australia's all-conquering netball team never relinquished control in a dominant victory over Games debutants the Tala at the Hydro.

Former Melbourne Mavericks goalscorer Uneeq Palavi was easily Tonga's biggest threat, but defensive midcourter Jamie-Lee Price did well to contain her ex-teammate.

The highly-rated Tongan attacker fired off 29 goals from 34 attempts as she managed being double-marked in the circle at times.

Palavi wasn't the only ex-Super Netball player on court, with former Queensland Firebirds midcourter Hulita Veve going head-to-head with Watson and Kate Moloney.

Price was one of five debutants in Australia's 12-strong squad, with Georgie Horjus, Matilda Garrett, Sophie Dwyer and Garbin all taking to the court.

Nailing the first step in Glasgow, the Diamonds will next face 2018 Gold Coast champions England in the second of five pool games.

Australia are aiming to go back-to-back for the second time in Games history since successfully defending their 1998 title in 2002.

The Diamonds have never missed a netball final since the sport was added to the Games program in 1998 and are the most successful nation with four gold medals.

It was just the second time the netball world No.1 played Tonga, having claimed an 85-38 pool victory at the 2023 World Cup in Cape Town.

Saturday's match may have been Tonga's first-ever Games match, but the Tala enjoyed healthy support from the nation's travelling contingent - which included Princess Latufuipeka Tuku'aho - and the Scottish home crowd.

item.title: Tonga’s women’s pairs secured a dramatic tie-break victory in section play
The Pacific's stake in shaping AI's future
item.description: By Kanni Wignaraja and Munkhtuya Altangerel Last week, governments from across the world gathered in Geneva for the first session of the UN Global Dialogue on AI Governance, and a presentation of the inaugural report of the Independent International Scientific Panel on AI . It marked an important step towards building global rules for artificial intelligence.
item.content:encoded:
By Kanni Wignaraja and Munkhtuya Altangerel

Last week, governments from across the world gathered in Geneva for the first session of the UN Global Dialogue on AI Governance, and a presentation of the inaugural report of the Independent International Scientific Panel on AI . It marked an important step towards building global rules for artificial intelligence.

While unpacking what AI can do for the Pacific, let us also consider what the Pacific can contribute to the future of AI . Both questions are relevant and connected, especially from a human development progress perspective.

The initial instinct, even anxiety, in small, remote economies could be to treat AI purely as a race from behind. And there is indeed need for that catch-up. So, the Kingdom of Tonga, for example, has moved through a national Digital Readiness Assessment, brought commercial 5G online, and is rebuilding its government services around a digital-first model, including AI tools designed to help citizens interact with the state in their own language.

Similar Digital Readiness Assessments have also been undertaken across Fiji, Samoa and Vanuatu, helping lay the foundations for AI adoption and digital transformation for the Pacific. This reflects strong national leadership and commitment across the government, with a willingness from the very top to jump into the race and speed up.

Foundational groundwork like this gives countries like Tonga real standing to speak on this issue from experience rather than aspiration. That includes investing in the AI skills and digital capabilities of people, to make the best use of the new data and services AI can offer.

However, framing the Pacific's AI challenge only as a catch-up exercise misses what the region is better placed to see than almost anywhere else. In Tonga, as across the Pacific, AI systems run into something they were not designed to encounter. Much of what local communities know about maritime navigation, weather, land and the ocean is oral, relational, and held collectively, passed down through practice and inter-generational responsibility rather than stored in a database. Some of it is sacred, and deliberately never written down.

The Pasifika Futures Report argues that the real question is not whether Pacific countries adopt AI , but whether technology supports the futures Pacific people want for themselves, especially younger generations. Digital Tuvalu offers perhaps the clearest example: a nation on the frontline of climate change using digital technology to preserve its culture, heritage and identity for generations to come, while advancing Simon Kofe's vision of a future in which Tuvaluans can connect with one another, explore their ancestry and culture, and access new opportunities for business and commerce.

This is not a barrier to AI adoption. It is an opportunity to shape how these technologies are designed and governed. Tonga is therefore well placed to bring this Pacific perspective to the future of AI , contributing views on identity, stewardship, culture and knowledge systems that remain largely absent from today's models and debates.

This brings up a larger missing piece in the current AI sphere – experiential and non-written knowledge and decisions, as well as intergenerational accountability, should not be viewed as peripheral considerations. They are critical inputs that remain largely absent from global AI governance discussions today. Ask the AI frameworks and models how they would treat a body of knowledge whose custodians choose not to digitise it, and the answer is that they were not built with this in mind. Not yet.

Tonga's own digital transformation gives it credibility to make this case precisely because it has not rushed. The Lagatoi Declaration, signed by Pacific ICT ministers in Port Moresby in 2023, set out a shared regional approach to digital transformation, infrastructure and governance long before AI dominated the conversation. Tonga's participation reflected a broader regional commitment: that a digitally connected Pacific should also be a secure and collaboratively governed one, built on shared standards rather than each nation solving the same problems alone.

What is now urgently needed is to deploy it. The Great Divergence that AI risks creating is not a distant concept. In March this year, Tonga hosted the Pacific launch of the report of that name, examining how the rapid acceleration of AI and digital technology is widening the gap between economies that build these systems and economies and societies that will simply live with the consequences.

Yet AI is already delivering results across the Pacific, from satellite and AI -enabled fisheries monitoring in Kiribati, which has helped recover around US $2 million annually in illegal fishing fines, to AI -assisted health diagnostics in countries including Nauru and Vanuatu. Digital innovation is advancing in Palau too, alongside partnerships with the European Union and UNCDF that are expanding digital services and AI -enabled financial inclusion across the region.

These are real wins, but they are wins within a system the Pacific did not design. The region already knows what it means to be on the wrong side of a divergence, in climate, in trade, in debt vulnerability. AI follows the same logic at greater speed. The difference is that the rules of AI are still being written, which means the divergence is not yet locked in. That window will not stay open for long. The time for the Pacific to shape the outcome is now, not once the frameworks are agreed and the tools are already being deployed.

The Pacific has spent decades demonstrating what it means to decide collectively, account for future generations, and treat traditional knowledge as sacred rather than extractive. These are not liabilities in the age of AI .

This is where a Pacific contribution can be pitched, while also driving for fairness in AI access and a gain in capabilities to even the odds in the AI race. Pacific representation in the forums shaping AI 's future can and must emphasise the distinction this region brings to shape AI models and applications of the future.

item.title: Kolomotu'a Eagles claim Pataloni Shield
item.description: The Kolomotu'a 'Ikale (Eagles) were awarded the Pataloni (Patrons) Shield as champions of the Tongatapu Sub-Union Pataloni title 2026 on Saturday after a closely contested grand final at Teufaiva Stadium. Kolomotu'a 'Ikale edged out Ha'ateiho Spartans 28-25 in the annual rugby union competition, which brings together clubs from across Tongatapu.
item.content:encoded:
The Kolomotu'a 'Ikale (Eagles) were awarded the Pataloni (Patrons) Shield as champions of the Tongatapu Sub-Union Pataloni title 2026 on Saturday after a closely contested grand final at Teufaiva Stadium.

Kolomotu'a 'Ikale edged out Ha'ateiho Spartans 28-25 in the annual rugby union competition, which brings together clubs from across Tongatapu.

Kolomotu'a prevailed in a head-to-head contest that remained in the balance until the closing stages, with the Eagles holding on to claim a three-point victory.

Supporters from both clubs packed Teufaiva Stadium, with strong backing for each side creating a vibrant atmosphere for the final.

The Pataloni Tournament is one of the Tongatapu Sub-Union's key competitions, providing local clubs with the opportunity to compete for the provincial title and showcase emerging rugby talent.

Following the final whistle, families and supporters of the Kolomotu'a side gathered on the field to celebrate the victory under clear and sunny conditions for the conclusion of another competitive season of sub-union rugby in Tongatapu.

item.title: Agricultural planning vital for food security during El Niño
item.description: Local authorities are encouraging farmers to plan and prepare for likely dry months ahead during El Niño season in Tonga, as a drought warning is in effect for the Ha'apai island groups, while the rest of Tonga is on a drought alert. Acting Director for the Ministry of Agriculture ( MAFF ) Dan Savia ‘Atuekaho stressed the risks of this El Niño to food security and livelihood for Tongans.
item.content:encoded:
Local authorities are encouraging farmers to plan and prepare for likely dry months ahead during El Niño season in Tonga, as a drought warning is in effect for the Ha'apai island groups, while the rest of Tonga is on a drought alert.

Acting Director for the Ministry of Agriculture ( MAFF ) Dan Savia ‘Atuekaho stressed the risks of this El Niño to food security and livelihood for Tongans.

‘Atuekaho told Matangi Tonga that farmers, fishermen, and households must be aware of the disaster that may follow.

" One of the biggest concern for Tonga is below-average rainfall. Most island groups, including Tongatapu, Vava’u and Ha’apai are expected to experience dry conditions," he said.

“The type of soil in Ha’apai is called sandy loam or known as tou’one. It is not able to retain water for a long period of time. Therefore, Ha’apai's agriculture is vulnerable [during drought] and differs from Tongatapu, which has a clay soil type. For Vava’u and other outer islands, the potential for water-holding capacity varies.”

He said there is also the risk of lower groundwater levels resulting in more saline soil, and if used for irrigation, it can damage crops.

He noted that key crops such a yam, cassava, taro, and watermelon are at risk of poor growth due to dry soils. He added that drought can lead to delayed planting season, lower crop yields, and increased pest and disease stress.

“Communities relying heavily on rainwater are particularly vulnerable.”

Meanwhile, 'Atuekaho expressed concern for livestock such as cattle, pigs, poultry which are affected by hotter and drier weather. "The possible impacts include, heat stress, reduced growth and productivity, limited pasture availabilities, and higher disease risks."

He mentioned that during the previous El Niño in 2025, some livestock around Tonga died from heat stress.

Last week, the Tonga Meteorological Services ( TMS ) announced a high likelihood for Tropical Cyclone ( TC ) activities affecting Tonga, with increased frequency of severe tropical cyclones category 3 to 5 expected during the upcoming tropical cyclone season, November 2026 - April 2027.

" These cyclones can cause crop destruction, flooding, damage to agricultural infrastructure, and loss of livestock."

On the other hand, marine and fisheries impacts from El Niño may cause coral bleaching, fish migration, and reduced coastal fish availability.

“Farmers, fishermen, and women should be ready and vigilant every year."

" Farmers should plant all year round. Farmers should grow crops to harvest before the cyclone season arrive," 'Atuekaho said.

“Agricultural planning is very important.”

item.content:encoded:
It is with considerable sadness that the Supreme Court of Tonga announces the death, on Saturday 18 July 2026, of the Hon. Kenneth (Ken) Handley AO CS tJ KC , a former Judge of the Court of Appeal of Tonga. He served on the Court of Appeal Bench for at least seven years until his retirement in 2019.

On the Bench, he was unfailingly courteous. Many of the judgments he authored for the Tongan Court of Appeal are noteworthy for their scholarship and all are marked by the precision of his writing. He was devoted to the interests of the Pacific and was a jurist of outstanding talent who served our Kingdom faithfully for many years. He did so with courtesy and with a steadfast desire to ensure that the interests of justice prevailed.

The Court also acknowledges with respect that he lived a long and distinguished life of 90 years, a life marked by service and devotion to justice.

The Supreme Court of Tonga extends its deepest condolences to his family as we remember a life well lived. May he rest in peace and rise in glory.

Hon. Malcolm Bishop KC Lord Chief Justice of the Kingdom of Tonga
